A compound collection is not a list; it has a shape. Some molecules huddle together in dense families, others sit alone in sparsely populated regions, and the biological activity we care about is spread unevenly across the whole. This unit is about seeing and exploiting that shape. We take more than a thousand real molecules measured against one protein target, turn each into the fingerprint vector of Unit 5, and then do three things a computer scientist will recognise immediately: we project the high-dimensional vectors into a two-dimensional picture (PCA, t-SNE, and conceptually UMAP), we cluster them, and we select a diverse subset. The chemistry is woven through: what "chemical space" means, why similar molecules cluster, and what a cluster's shared scaffold tells a medicinal chemist. Nothing here needs a protein structure, a docking engine or a GPU - it is pure ligand-based cheminformatics, and every figure is produced by a few seconds of computation.

Learning objectives

  • Explain what "chemical space" is, why it is astronomically large, and why fingerprints give it a usable geometry.
  • Project a fingerprint set into 2-D with PCA and t-SNE, and read the resulting map critically - knowing what each method preserves and what it distorts.
  • State the Taylor-Butina sphere-exclusion algorithm, trace it by hand on a small distance matrix, and run it on a real dataset of over a thousand molecules with RDKit.
  • Relate clusters to Bemis-Murcko scaffolds and read the dominant chemotype of a congeneric series out of a cluster.
  • Select a maximally diverse subset (a MaxMin "plate") and justify a diversity pick against a random one with a nearest-neighbour argument.
  • Colour a chemical-space map by activity and recognise - without over-interpreting - where potency concentrates.

How to read this notebook

Run each code cell as you reach it and read its output before moving on; the prose after a figure tells you the numbers to look for. Green chemistry boxes define each chemical term in plain language the first time it appears. The only library you must install in Google Colab is RDKit (!pip install rdkit); NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn and matplotlib are already there. This unit builds directly on Unit 5 (fingerprints and Tanimoto similarity) and reuses the unsupervised-learning intuition - PCA, t-SNE, k-means - from the companion AI course; we recall each idea briefly but do not re-derive it.

1. What is "chemical space"?

Chemistry box - chemical space, scaffold, series

Chemical space is the set of all possible molecules, together with some notion of which molecules are "close" to which. It is the chemist's analogue of a feature space: every molecule is a point, and nearby points are structurally similar. A scaffold (or chemotype) is the core ring system of a molecule once its peripheral groups are stripped away - think of it as the shared skeleton of a family. A series (or congeneric set) is a group of molecules built on one scaffold by a medicinal chemist varying the substituents; a series is exactly the kind of tight cluster we will find. An assay is a laboratory experiment that measures how strongly a molecule acts on a biological target (usually a protein); IC50 is the concentration that halves the target's activity - smaller means more potent.

Chemical space is unimaginably large. The enumerated database GDB-17 contains 166 billion organic molecules with up to 17 heavy atoms built from C, N, O, S and halogens[2]; estimates for drug-like molecules up to ~500 g/mol run to 1033 or more[4]. By contrast, every molecule ever made and recorded is of order 108, and a public bioactivity database such as ChEMBL holds a few million[21][22]; the aggregator PubChem[23] and the purchasable-compound catalogue ZINC[24] are larger still, and Unit 6 covers all of them. The practical consequence is stark: we have sampled a vanishing fraction of what is chemically possible[3], so navigation, interpolation and diversity selection matter enormously. Systematic attempts to chart and enumerate this space - the Chemical Space Project being the most ambitious[1] - are a research field in their own right, and the project-level maps we build in this unit are the small-scale version of the same ambition. For a computer scientist the motivation is sharper still: chemical-space analysis is increasingly the front end of machine-learning pipelines for drug discovery[27][28], because how you sample, split and cluster a library silently determines what any downstream model can learn and how honestly it can be evaluated (Unit 14). The cell below puts those magnitudes on one logarithmic axis.

# The scales of chemical space, on a log axis (counts are literature estimates, cited in the text).
scales = [
    ("a 96-well plate",            96),
    ("one ChEMBL target (this unit)", 2000),
    ("approved small-molecule drugs", 2_000),
    ("ChEMBL compounds",           2_400_000),
    ("PubChem compounds",          115_000_000),
    ("GDB-17 (<=17 heavy atoms)",  166_000_000_000),
    ("drug-like space (estimate)", 1e33),
]
labels = [s[0] for s in scales]; vals = [s[1] for s in scales]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2, 3.2))
ax.barh(range(len(vals)), np.log10(vals), color="#4a7fb5")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(vals))); ax.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=8)
ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_xlabel("log10(number of molecules)")
ax.set_title("Chemical space spans ~30 orders of magnitude")
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(np.log10(v) + 0.3, i, f"$10^{{{np.log10(v):.0f}}}$", va="center", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 38)
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 1. The sizes involved, each bar the base-10 logarithm of a count. The jump from what has been synthesised (left) to what is enumerable (GDB-17) to what is estimated possible (right) is about thirty orders of magnitude. A medicinal-chemistry project explores the tiny sliver on the far left; the methods in this unit are how we make that sliver count - by mapping it, clustering it and sampling it well rather than blindly.

A map of chemical space is only as good as the notion of distance it is built on. In Unit 5 we turned a molecule into a Morgan fingerprint: a long binary vector whose bits record which circular atom-environments are present, and we measured similarity with the Tanimoto coefficient (the size of the bit intersection over the union)[6][7]. That fingerprint-plus-Tanimoto geometry is what we will visualise, cluster and sample. Everything in this unit therefore inherits a single assumption - the similar-property principle[9]: molecules with similar structures tend to have similar properties. We will both use that principle and watch it fail.

2. Getting a real dataset: EGFR inhibitors from ChEMBL

Chemistry box - target, kinase, IC50 and pIC50

Our running example is the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), a kinase - an enzyme that attaches phosphate groups to other proteins and that, when overactive, drives several cancers. Molecules that block it (EGFR inhibitors such as gefitinib and erlotinib) are real drugs. For each molecule ChEMBL stores an IC50: the concentration (here in nanomolar, nM) that halves the enzyme's activity. Because IC50 spans many orders of magnitude, we convert it to pIC50 = -log10(IC50 in molar) = 9 - log10(IC50 in nM); a pIC50 of 9 is 1 nM (very potent), 6 is 1 micromolar (weak). pIC50 is the activity we colour our maps by.

The next cell fetches a slice of EGFR IC50 measurements from the ChEMBL REST web service. It is wrapped in try/except: when the notebook runs in Colab (or here, if the network allows) it pulls live data; if the service is slow or unreachable it falls back to a small bundled set of real EGFR-active SMILES so the notebook always runs. We keep only exact ("=") IC50 values in nM, take the median per compound, and convert to pIC50.

# Fetch EGFR (CHEMBL203) IC50 data from ChEMBL REST; fall back to a bundled sample if the network fails.
def fetch_chembl_egfr(npages=2, page=1000, timeout=25):
    base = "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/api/data/activity.json"
    only = "canonical_smiles,molecule_chembl_id,standard_value,standard_units,standard_type,standard_relation"
    rows, off = [], 0
    for _ in range(npages):
        url = (f"{base}?target_chembl_id=CHEMBL203&standard_type=IC50&standard_relation=%3D"
               f"&limit={page}&offset={off}&only={only}")
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "python-urllib"})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as r:
            d = json.load(r)
        rows += d["activities"]; off += page
        if not d["page_meta"]["next"]:
            break
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

3. From molecules to a geometry: fingerprints and Tanimoto distance

Before we can map or cluster, each molecule must become a vector. We use the Morgan fingerprint of Unit 5: for each atom we hash its circular environment out to a chosen radius, and set the corresponding bits of a fixed-length vector[6]. A computer scientist can read it as a feature hash of the molecular graph. We use radius 2 (ECFP4-like) and 2048 bits throughout. Every structural computation in this unit - fingerprints, Tanimoto distances, Butina clustering and scaffold extraction - is done with RDKit[26]; the projections (PCA, t-SNE) and k-means come from scikit-learn, so the whole pipeline runs in Colab with a single extra install.

Chemistry box - the fingerprint is the coordinate system

Everything downstream - the 2-D map, the clusters, the diversity pick - is computed on these bit vectors, not on the molecules themselves. The fingerprint is the chemistry as far as the algorithms are concerned. If the fingerprint cannot tell two molecules apart (a known limitation for stereochemistry, for instance), no amount of clever projection will. Choosing the representation is the most consequential decision in the whole pipeline; we revisit its limits in Unit 14.

# Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2048 bits) for every molecule; summarise their bit density.
mfpgen = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=2048)
fps = [mfpgen.GetFingerprint(m) for m in mols]
onbits = np.array([fp.GetNumOnBits() for fp in fps])
# dense 0/1 matrix for PCA / k-means (a few MB for 1500 x 2048)
X = np.zeros((N, 2048), dtype=np.uint8)
for i, fp in enumerate(fps):
    DataStructs.ConvertToNumpyArray(fp, X[i])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
ax.hist(onbits, bins=40, color="#4a7fb5")
ax.axvline(onbits.mean(), color="#d2691e", lw=1.5, label=f"mean {onbits.mean():.0f} bits")
ax.set_xlabel("number of bits set ('on') per molecule"); ax.set_ylabel("molecules")
ax.set_title("Fingerprints are sparse: ~%d of 2048 bits set" % onbits.mean()); ax.legend(frameon=False)
print(f"mean {onbits.mean():.1f} on-bits of 2048 ({100*onbits.mean()/2048:.1f}%); "
      f"range {onbits.min()}-{onbits.max()}")
fig.tight_layout()

mean 46.5 on-bits of 2048 (2.3%); range 20-85

Figure 2. How many of the 2048 bits each molecule switches on. The mean is only a few dozen, so the fingerprint matrix is extremely sparse - typically a percent or two of entries are non-zero. Sparsity is why Tanimoto (which looks only at bits that are on in at least one molecule) is the natural similarity measure and why Euclidean distance on the raw bits is almost useless: two random drug-like molecules share almost no bits, so they are nearly equidistant. This is the curse of dimensionality in concrete form, and the reason we both reduce dimensions and use a set-overlap distance.

We measure distance between two fingerprints as 1 - Tanimoto similarity. Tanimoto is bounded in [0, 1], so Tanimoto distance is too: 0 means identical bit sets, 1 means no shared bits. The cell builds the full N x N distance matrix once (RDKit's bulk routine makes this fast) - we reuse it for both t-SNE and clustering - and shows the distribution of pairwise distances.

# Full Tanimoto-distance matrix (reused by t-SNE and Butina); plot the distribution of pairwise distances.
D = np.zeros((N, N), dtype=np.float32)
for i in range(N):
    sims = DataStructs.BulkTanimotoSimilarity(fps[i], fps)
    D[i] = 1.0 - np.array(sims, dtype=np.float32)
iu = np.triu_indices(N, k=1)
pair = D[iu]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
ax.hist(pair, bins=50, color="#4a7fb5")
ax.axvline(np.median(pair), color="#d2691e", lw=1.5, label=f"median {np.median(pair):.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("pairwise Tanimoto distance (1 - similarity)"); ax.set_ylabel("molecule pairs")
ax.set_title("Most molecule pairs are far apart"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
print(f"{len(pair):,} pairs | median distance {np.median(pair):.3f} | "
      f"fraction with similarity>=0.6 (distance<=0.4): {(pair<=0.4).mean()*100:.1f}%")
fig.tight_layout()

878,475 pairs | median distance 0.870 | fraction with similarity>=0.6 (distance<=0.4): 0.8%

Figure 3. The distribution of all pairwise Tanimoto distances in the set. The mass sits far to the right (median distance near 0.9): the overwhelming majority of pairs are dissimilar, and only a small percentage are genuinely close (similarity >= 0.6). A compound collection is mostly empty space with a few dense neighbourhoods - precisely the structure that clustering exists to find and that a 2-D map tries to lay out faithfully.

3.1 The similar-property principle, and where it breaks

The assumption underpinning every method here is that structurally similar molecules have similar activity[9]. That same principle is the engine of ligand-based virtual screening, where a large library is ranked by fingerprint similarity to a known active and the top of the list is tested first[8][30]; here we use it not to rank but to understand a collection's shape. We can test it directly: for many random pairs, plot the absolute difference in pIC50 against the pair's similarity. If the principle held perfectly, similar pairs (right) would show small activity differences.

# Similar-property principle: activity difference vs similarity for a random sample of pairs.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = rng.integers(0, N, (4000, 2))
idx = idx[idx[:, 0] != idx[:, 1]]
sim = 1.0 - D[idx[:, 0], idx[:, 1]]
dact = np.abs(data.pIC50.values[idx[:, 0]] - data.pIC50.values[idx[:, 1]])
bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 11); mid = (bins[:-1] + bins[1:]) / 2
which = np.digitize(sim, bins) - 1
mean_d = [dact[which == b].mean() if (which == b).any() else np.nan for b in range(10)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 3.2))
ax.scatter(sim, dact, s=4, alpha=0.15, color="#4a7fb5")
ax.plot(mid, mean_d, "o-", color="#d2691e", lw=2, label="mean |delta pIC50| per similarity bin")
ax.set_xlabel("Tanimoto similarity of the pair"); ax.set_ylabel("|difference in pIC50|")
ax.set_title("Similar molecules usually - but not always - act alike"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
print("mean |delta pIC50| for similarity<0.3: %.2f | for similarity>0.7: %.2f"
      % (dact[sim < 0.3].mean(), dact[sim > 0.7].mean() if (sim > 0.7).any() else float("nan")))
fig.tight_layout()

mean |delta pIC50| for similarity<0.3: 1.80 | for similarity>0.7: 0.74

Figure 4. Each grey point is a pair of molecules; the orange line is the mean activity difference within bins of similarity. The trend is the similar-property principle at work: as similarity rises (moving right), the average difference in potency falls. But the scatter never collapses to zero - some very similar pairs still differ by orders of magnitude in activity. Those are activity cliffs[9]: tiny structural changes with huge activity consequences, the single most important failure mode of similarity-based reasoning and the subject of Unit 11. Keep them in mind: a smooth, pretty chemical-space map can hide cliffs, because two points placed next to each other need not be equipotent.

4. Projecting to 2-D (I): Principal Component Analysis

A fingerprint lives in 2048 dimensions; we have two to draw with. Dimensionality reduction finds a low-dimensional layout that keeps as much of the structure as possible. The linear baseline is Principal Component Analysis (PCA): it finds the orthogonal directions of greatest variance and projects onto the first few[10]. You met PCA in the AI course; here we simply apply it to the fingerprint matrix. PCA is fast, deterministic and - crucially - its axes are interpretable distances, so relative positions on a PCA map are meaningful in a way they are not for the methods that follow.

Concretely, PCA diagonalises the covariance matrix of the feature vectors: the first principal component is the single direction along which the molecules vary most, the second is the most-varying direction orthogonal to the first, and so on. Projecting onto the first two gives the best possible two-dimensional picture in the least-squares sense - no linear map can preserve more of the total variance in two dimensions. That optimality is also PCA's weakness here: "best linear" is only good when a few directions dominate, and we have already seen that fingerprint variance does not concentrate that way. The percentages printed on the axes are therefore the key diagnostic, not decoration.

# PCA of the fingerprint matrix to 2 components; scatter coloured by activity (pIC50).
pca = PCA(n_components=10, random_state=0).fit(X.astype(np.float32))
P = pca.transform(X.astype(np.float32))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.6))
sc = ax.scatter(P[:, 0], P[:, 1], c=data.pIC50, cmap="viridis", s=12, alpha=0.8)
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax); cb.set_label("pIC50 (higher = more potent)")
ax.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100:.1f}% of variance)")
ax.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100:.1f}% of variance)")
ax.set_title("PCA map of EGFR chemical space, coloured by potency")
print("variance explained by PC1, PC2: %.1f%%, %.1f%% (cumulative %.1f%%)"
      % (pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100, pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100,
         pca.explained_variance_ratio_[:2].sum()*100))
fig.tight_layout()

variance explained by PC1, PC2: 11.9%, 4.7% (cumulative 16.7%)

Figure 5. The PCA projection, each point a molecule coloured by pIC50. The percentages on the axes are the fraction of total variance each component captures - and even the first two together explain only a modest share (the printout gives the exact split; here well under a quarter). That is the honest headline of PCA on fingerprints: because the variance is spread across many directions with no small dominant set, two linear axes cannot summarise it well, so the picture looks like a diffuse cloud. Regions of higher potency (yellow) are visible but not cleanly separated. PCA tells us the data is genuinely high-dimensional; it does not give a satisfying map. The scree plot next makes the diagnosis explicit.

# Scree plot: how much variance the leading principal components capture.
ev = pca.explained_variance_ratio_ * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
ax.bar(np.arange(1, 11), ev, color="#4a7fb5")
ax.plot(np.arange(1, 11), np.cumsum(ev), "o-", color="#d2691e", label="cumulative")
ax.set_xlabel("principal component"); ax.set_ylabel("% of variance")
ax.set_title("Scree plot: variance is spread thin across many directions")
ax.legend(frameon=False); ax.set_xticks(range(1, 11))
print("cumulative variance in first 10 PCs: %.1f%%" % np.cumsum(ev)[-1])
fig.tight_layout()

cumulative variance in first 10 PCs: 39.9%

Figure 6. The variance captured by each of the first ten principal components (bars) and the running total (line). Even ten components together account for only a modest fraction of the variance - the curve climbs slowly. A molecular fingerprint space has no small set of dominant directions; it is intrinsically high-dimensional. This is exactly the setting where non-linear neighbour-preserving methods earn their keep, because they give up on faithful global geometry in exchange for revealing local structure.

5. Projecting to 2-D (II): t-SNE

t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding (t-SNE) abandons the goal of preserving all distances and instead preserves neighbourhoods: it places points so that each molecule's nearest neighbours in fingerprint space stay nearby in 2-D, while deliberately letting far-apart points land anywhere[11]. The result is a map that separates clusters crisply - far better for the eye than PCA - at the cost of global meaning. We feed t-SNE our precomputed Tanimoto distance matrix so it works on exactly the chemistry-aware distance we clustered on.

The mechanism is worth one sentence of intuition, because it explains every caveat. t-SNE converts distances into probabilities - for each molecule, the chance of picking each other molecule as a neighbour - and then arranges the 2-D points so that their neighbour-probabilities match the high-dimensional ones as closely as possible (it minimises the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the two, the number printed by the cell). Because the objective only cares about getting neighbourhoods right, it is free to place unrelated groups wherever is convenient, which is precisely why global distances on the map carry no information. PCA asks "what are the main axes of variation?"; t-SNE asks "who is next to whom?" - two different questions with two different, non-interchangeable answers.

How to read a t-SNE map honestly

Three rules, because t-SNE is the most over-interpreted plot in cheminformatics. (1) Cluster sizes mean nothing - t-SNE expands dense regions and shrinks sparse ones. (2) Distances between clusters mean nothing - two clusters placed far apart are not more different than two placed close. (3) The result is stochastic and depends on perplexity - a hyperparameter that sets the effective neighbourhood size. Trust which points group together; distrust everything about the global arrangement. We demonstrate the perplexity dependence immediately after.

# t-SNE on the precomputed Tanimoto-distance matrix; colour by activity.
ts = TSNE(n_components=2, metric="precomputed", init="random",
          perplexity=30, random_state=0, max_iter=1000)
Y = ts.fit_transform(D.astype(np.float64))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.6))
sc = ax.scatter(Y[:, 0], Y[:, 1], c=data.pIC50, cmap="viridis", s=12, alpha=0.8)
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax); cb.set_label("pIC50 (higher = more potent)")
ax.set_xlabel("t-SNE 1 (no units)"); ax.set_ylabel("t-SNE 2 (no units)")
ax.set_title("t-SNE map of EGFR chemical space, coloured by potency")
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
print("t-SNE embedded", Y.shape[0], "molecules; KL divergence %.2f" % ts.kl_divergence_)
fig.tight_layout()

t-SNE embedded 1326 molecules; KL divergence 0.58

Figure 7. The same molecules under t-SNE. Compared with the PCA cloud, discrete islands now appear - each is a set of mutually similar molecules, typically a chemical series. Crucially, several islands are fairly uniform in colour: potency is not scattered at random but concentrates in particular structural families, which is the medicinal-chemistry payoff of the map. Remember the warning box: read the membership of each island, not its size or its distance from other islands. The axes are deliberately unlabelled and unitless because their scale is meaningless.

# Perplexity sensitivity: the SAME data at perplexity 5 and 50 gives visibly different maps.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.0, 4.2))
for ax, perp in zip(axes, [5, 50]):
    Yp = TSNE(n_components=2, metric="precomputed", init="random",
              perplexity=perp, random_state=0, max_iter=1000).fit_transform(D.astype(np.float64))
    ax.scatter(Yp[:, 0], Yp[:, 1], c=data.pIC50, cmap="viridis", s=8, alpha=0.8)
    ax.set_title(f"perplexity = {perp}"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.suptitle("Same molecules, same seed - different perplexity, different map", y=1.02, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 8. One dataset, one random seed, two perplexities. Low perplexity (left) emphasises very local structure and shatters the data into many small fragments; high perplexity (right) emphasises broader neighbourhoods and merges them into fewer, larger blobs. Neither is "the truth": the apparent number and separation of clusters is partly an artefact of a knob you chose. Reading structure into a projection that is not really there is a form of fooling yourself - the visual cousin of overfitting[29] - and it is remarkably easy to do with a map that looks convincing. This is why a t-SNE picture must never be the sole evidence for a claim about chemical space - it is a hypothesis generator, to be confirmed by an algorithm with a defined criterion, such as the clustering we turn to next.

6. Projecting to 2-D (III): UMAP, in concept

Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is the third method you will meet everywhere in modern cheminformatics[12]. Like t-SNE it is a non-linear neighbour-preserving embedding, but it is built on a different mathematical footing (a fuzzy topological representation of the data) and in practice it is faster, scales to millions of points, and tends to preserve a little more of the global structure than t-SNE. Its hyperparameters are the number of neighbours (analogous to perplexity) and a minimum-distance that controls how tightly points pack. For very large libraries, specialised layouts such as TMAP[18] and interactive tools such as DataWarrior[20] and ChemMaps[19] extend the same idea. Neighbour-preserving projection is itself only one family of map-makers: the self-organizing map[13], which fits a low-dimensional grid of prototype vectors to the data, was an early and still-used alternative for charting chemical space, and it shares the same health warning - the grid imposes a topology that may not match the data's.

UMAP ships in the umap-learn package, which is not part of the Colab/RDKit default set and is not reliably importable in the environment that builds this page. The cell below therefore attempts to import and run UMAP and, if it cannot, states so and proceeds - the t-SNE map already illustrates every reading rule UMAP would. To run UMAP yourself, pip install umap-learn and the same distance matrix feeds straight in.

# Attempt UMAP; fall back gracefully if umap-learn is unavailable in this environment.
umap_status = None
try:
    import umap  # noqa: F401
    reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, metric="precomputed", random_state=0)
    U = reducer.fit_transform(D.astype(np.float64))
    umap_status = f"UMAP ran: embedded {U.shape[0]} molecules"
except Exception as e:
    U = None
    umap_status = f"UMAP unavailable here ({type(e).__name__}); using PCA + t-SNE, as the unit describes."
print(umap_status)

UMAP unavailable here (RuntimeError); using PCA + t-SNE, as the unit describes.

The printout states which path executed. When UMAP is present the embedding U can be scatter-plotted exactly like the t-SNE map; when it is absent - as in this build - we lose nothing pedagogically, because the three reading rules of the warning box apply verbatim to UMAP. The lesson is methodological, not package-specific: every non-linear projection trades global faithfulness for local clarity, so treat all of them as hypothesis generators.

7. Clustering (I): the Taylor-Butina algorithm

A map suggests groups; clustering defines them with a reproducible rule. The field's default for fingerprints is Taylor-Butina sphere exclusion[14][15], because it needs only a distance threshold (not a pre-chosen number of clusters), it is deterministic, and it names an explicit centroid for every cluster. It works on the Tanimoto distances we already have.

Chemistry box - what a cluster is for

Clustering a compound set groups molecules that share a chemotype. A medicinal chemist uses this to (i) see how many distinct structural ideas a screening hit list actually contains - fifty molecules might be three series in disguise; (ii) pick one representative per cluster to avoid testing near-duplicates; and (iii) spot which chemotype is enriched among the actives. The cluster centroid is the natural representative.

The algorithm

Given a distance threshold t (molecules closer than t are "neighbours"):

  1. For every molecule, count how many neighbours it has (how many others lie within t).
  2. Sort molecules by neighbour count, most-connected first.
  3. Take the most-connected unassigned molecule as a new cluster centroid; put it and all its still-unassigned neighbours into that cluster and mark them assigned ("exclude the sphere" of radius t around the centroid).
  4. Repeat step 3 on the remaining unassigned molecules until none are left; molecules that were never anyone's neighbour end up as singleton clusters.

This is a greedy cover: each pass claims the densest remaining sphere. The next section traces it by hand before we unleash it on the full set.

7.1 Worked example by hand

Take six small molecules - phenol, catechol, aniline, ethanol, 1-propanol and toluene - and their Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto distance matrix (rounded to two decimals):

phenolcatecholanilineethanolpropanoltoluene
phenol0.000.500.620.940.940.62
catechol0.500.000.690.930.940.69
aniline0.620.690.001.001.000.62
ethanol0.940.931.000.000.440.94
propanol0.940.941.000.440.000.94
toluene0.620.690.620.940.940.00

Use threshold t = 0.65 (molecules closer than 0.65 are neighbours).

Step 1 - neighbour counts. Reading each row for entries <= 0.65 (ignoring the zero on the diagonal):

  • phenol: catechol (0.50), aniline (0.62), toluene (0.62) -> 3 neighbours
  • aniline: phenol (0.62), toluene (0.62) -> 2 (catechol is 0.69, just over)
  • toluene: phenol (0.62), aniline (0.62) -> 2 (catechol is 0.69)
  • catechol: phenol (0.50) -> 1 (aniline/toluene are 0.69)
  • ethanol: propanol (0.44) -> 1
  • propanol: ethanol (0.44) -> 1

Step 2 - sort: phenol (3), aniline (2), toluene (2), catechol (1), ethanol (1), propanol (1).

Step 3 - first sphere: phenol is most connected, so it becomes the first centroid. Its unassigned neighbours are catechol, aniline and toluene, so Cluster 1 = {phenol, catechol, aniline, toluene}. All four are now assigned (even though catechol and aniline were not within 0.65 of each other, they are swept in because they are within 0.65 of the centroid - that is the "sphere exclusion" rule).

Step 3 again: the most-connected unassigned molecules are ethanol and propanol - a genuine tie, since each is the other's only neighbour, so either may serve as centroid (RDKit's implementation happens to pick propanol). Whichever is chosen sweeps in the other, giving Cluster 2 = {ethanol, propanol}. Nothing remains.

Result: two clusters, an aromatic one and an aliphatic one - chemically exactly right. The cell confirms the membership with RDKit's implementation.

# Confirm the hand trace with RDKit's Butina on the same six molecules.
names6 = ["phenol", "catechol", "aniline", "ethanol", "propanol", "toluene"]
smis6 = ["c1ccccc1O", "Oc1ccccc1O", "c1ccccc1N", "CCO", "CCCO", "Cc1ccccc1"]
fps6 = [mfpgen.GetFingerprint(Chem.MolFromSmiles(s)) for s in smis6]
n6 = len(fps6)
d6 = [1 - DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fps6[i], fps6[j]) for i in range(n6) for j in range(i)]
# neighbour counts at t=0.65 (reproducing step 1)
D6 = np.array([[1 - DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(a, b) for b in fps6] for a in fps6])
counts = {names6[i]: int(((D6[i] <= 0.65).sum() - 1)) for i in range(n6)}
print("neighbour counts:", counts)
clusters6 = Butina.ClusterData(d6, n6, 0.65, isDistData=True)
for k, c in enumerate(clusters6, 1):
    print(f"cluster {k}: centroid={names6[c[0]]:9s} members={[names6[i] for i in c]}")

neighbour counts: {'phenol': 3, 'catechol': 1, 'aniline': 2, 'ethanol': 1, 'propanol': 1, 'toluene': 2}
cluster 1: centroid=phenol    members=['phenol', 'catechol', 'aniline', 'toluene']
cluster 2: centroid=propanol  members=['propanol', 'ethanol']

The neighbour counts match the hand trace exactly (phenol 3; aniline and toluene 2; the rest 1), and RDKit returns the same two clusters - an aromatic cluster whose centroid is the most-connected phenol, and an aliphatic pair. Having verified our understanding on six molecules, we apply the identical procedure to the full EGFR set.

7.2 Butina on the full set

We feed the lower triangle of the distance matrix D to RDKit and cluster at a distance threshold of 0.4 (Tanimoto similarity >= 0.6) - a common choice for ECFP4-like fingerprints that keeps genuine series together without merging unrelated chemotypes.

The threshold is the one real decision in Butina, and it is worth dwelling on. Loosen it (allow more distant neighbours) and clusters grow and merge until, at the extreme, everything collapses into one blob; tighten it and clusters splinter until every molecule is its own singleton. There is no universally correct value - it encodes what you mean by "the same series" for the task at hand. A sensible habit is to report the threshold alongside the cluster count (as we do in the printout) and, for a decision that matters, to check that your conclusion is stable across a small range of thresholds rather than an artefact of one lucky cut.

# Cluster the full set with Taylor-Butina at distance threshold 0.4 (similarity >= 0.6).
CUTOFF = 0.4
condensed = D[np.tril_indices(N, -1)].astype(np.float64).tolist()
clusters = Butina.ClusterData(condensed, N, CUTOFF, isDistData=True)
clusters = sorted(clusters, key=len, reverse=True)
sizes = np.array([len(c) for c in clusters])
cluster_of = np.empty(N, dtype=int)
for ci, c in enumerate(clusters):
    for i in c:
        cluster_of[i] = ci
n_singletons = int((sizes == 1).sum())
print(f"{len(clusters)} clusters at cutoff {CUTOFF} | largest {sizes[0]} molecules | "
      f"singletons {n_singletons} ({100*n_singletons/len(clusters):.0f}% of clusters) | "
      f"top-5 sizes {sizes[:5].tolist()}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 3.2))
ax.bar(range(1, min(31, len(sizes) + 1)), sizes[:30], color="#4a7fb5")
ax.set_xlabel("cluster rank (largest first)"); ax.set_ylabel("molecules in cluster")
ax.set_title(f"Cluster-size distribution ({len(clusters)} clusters, top 30 shown)")
fig.tight_layout()

334 clusters at cutoff 0.4 | largest 71 molecules | singletons 168 (50% of clusters) | top-5 sizes [71, 47, 38, 37, 31]

Figure 9. The size of each cluster, largest first (top 30 of the full set). The distribution is the one every compound collection shows: a few populous clusters - the well-explored chemical series a project has invested in - followed by a long tail of small clusters and many singletons (isolated molecules with no close neighbour at this threshold). The exact numbers are printed above the figure. The shape, not the particular counts, is the lesson: real libraries are a handful of dense series embedded in a sea of one-offs, and the fraction of singletons is a blunt diversity index.

# Overlay the clustering on the t-SNE map: colour the largest clusters, grey the rest.
TOPK = 8
palette = plt.cm.tab10(np.linspace(0, 1, 10))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.8))
rest = cluster_of >= TOPK
ax.scatter(Y[rest, 0], Y[rest, 1], s=8, color="#cccccc", alpha=0.6, label="smaller clusters")
for ci in range(TOPK):
    sel = cluster_of == ci
    ax.scatter(Y[sel, 0], Y[sel, 1], s=16, color=palette[ci], label=f"cluster {ci+1} (n={sizes[ci]})")
ax.set_title("Butina clusters on the t-SNE map"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.legend(fontsize=6.5, frameon=False, loc="upper left", ncol=2)
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 10. The Butina clusters painted onto the t-SNE layout. The two methods agree encouragingly: the largest Butina clusters land as compact, single-colour islands on the t-SNE map, even though t-SNE never saw the cluster labels and Butina never saw the 2-D coordinates. This cross-check is the right way to use a projection - as independent corroboration of an algorithm that has a defined criterion, rather than as standalone evidence. Where the two disagree (a Butina cluster split across the map, or one island holding two colours) you have found a place where the 2-D layout is lying, exactly as the warning box predicted.

7.3 A contrast: k-means

k-means, the clustering you met in the AI course, is a useful foil. It partitions the fingerprint vectors into a pre-chosen number k of groups by minimising within-group Euclidean variance. Unlike Butina it needs k in advance, it has no notion of a centroid molecule (its centroid is an average bit vector, not a real compound), and Euclidean distance on sparse bits is exactly the measure we argued is weak. We run it at the Butina cluster count to compare.

# k-means at k = number of Butina clusters, shown on the same t-SNE map for comparison.
k = min(len(clusters), 40)
km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(X.astype(np.float32))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 4.4))
axes[0].scatter(Y[:, 0], Y[:, 1], c=cluster_of, cmap="tab20", s=8, alpha=0.8)
axes[0].set_title(f"Taylor-Butina ({len(clusters)} clusters)")
axes[1].scatter(Y[:, 0], Y[:, 1], c=km.labels_, cmap="tab20", s=8, alpha=0.8)
axes[1].set_title(f"k-means (k={k})")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.suptitle("Two clusterings of the same molecules", y=1.02, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
print(f"Butina: {len(clusters)} clusters, defined centroids, no k needed | k-means: k={k} fixed in advance")
fig.tight_layout()

Butina: 334 clusters, defined centroids, no k needed | k-means: k=40 fixed in advance

Figure 11. Butina (left) versus k-means (right) on the same t-SNE layout. Both recover the obvious islands, but their characters differ: Butina leaves sparse regions as many singletons and gives each cluster a real representative molecule, whereas k-means must assign every molecule to one of exactly k groups, so it slices through sparse regions and can split a single visual island or merge two. For picking representatives and for diversity work, the explicit-centroid, threshold-based Butina is usually preferred in cheminformatics; k-means remains handy when you genuinely want a fixed number of balanced groups.

8. Reading scaffolds out of the clusters

A cluster is only useful if we can say what its members have in common. The standard answer is the Bemis-Murcko scaffold: strip every terminal substituent and keep the ring systems plus the linkers between them[17]. Molecules in one tight cluster usually share a scaffold - that shared core is the chemical series. Scaffolds are so central to how chemists organise structures that the diversity of the entire CAS Registry of known organic chemistry has been analysed through them[5], finding that a small number of frameworks account for a large share of all known molecules - the same few-dense-many-sparse pattern our clusters show, now at the scale of all of chemistry.

Chemistry box - scaffold, in one picture

Take a molecule, delete the dangling groups (the methyls, halogens, hydroxyls at the edges) and you are left with its skeleton of rings and the bonds joining them. That skeleton is the Murcko scaffold. Two drugs with the same scaffold are "the same idea with different decoration"; swapping decorations while keeping the scaffold is the daily work of lead optimisation (Unit 11).

# The Murcko scaffold of each large cluster's centroid - the shared core of each series.
def scaffold_smiles(mol):
    core = MurckoScaffold.GetScaffoldForMol(mol)
    return Chem.MolToSmiles(core) if core.GetNumAtoms() else Chem.MolToSmiles(mol)
top = [c for c in clusters if len(c) >= 5][:6]
scaff_mols, legends = [], []
for rank, c in enumerate(top, 1):
    centroid = mols[c[0]]
    sm = scaffold_smiles(centroid)
    scaff_mols.append(Chem.MolFromSmiles(sm))
    legends.append(f"cluster {rank} (n={len(c)})")
for rank, c in enumerate(top, 1):
    print(f"cluster {rank}: n={len(c):4d}  centroid scaffold = {scaffold_smiles(mols[c[0]])}")
Draw.MolsToGridImage(scaff_mols, molsPerRow=3, subImgSize=(230, 170), legends=legends)

cluster 1: n=  71  centroid scaffold = c1ccc(Nc2ncnc3ccccc23)cc1
cluster 2: n=  47  centroid scaffold = c1ccc(Nc2ncnc3ccccc23)cc1
cluster 3: n=  38  centroid scaffold = c1ccc(CNc2ccccc2)cc1
cluster 4: n=  37  centroid scaffold = c1ccc(Nc2ncnc3cnccc23)cc1
cluster 5: n=  31  centroid scaffold = c1ccc(Nc2ncnc3ccc(OCCCN4CCOCC4)cc23)cc1
cluster 6: n=  31  centroid scaffold = O=C1NCc2c1c1c3ccccc3n3c1c1c2c2ccccc2n1C1CCC[C@H]3O1

Figure 12. The Bemis-Murcko scaffold of the centroid of each of the largest clusters. Several are variations on a quinazoline core (a fused two-ring aromatic system with two nitrogens) - the classic EGFR-inhibitor chemotype shared by the drugs gefitinib and erlotinib - which is exactly what we should recover from an EGFR dataset, and a reassuring sanity check that the pipeline has found real chemistry rather than fingerprint noise. Each scaffold is the skeleton that the dozens of molecules in its cluster decorate differently; naming it turns an anonymous cluster into a medicinal-chemistry series.

# The members of the single largest cluster: one series, many decorations.
big = clusters[0]
show = list(big[:9])
gal = [mols[i] for i in show]
legs = [f"pIC50 {data.pIC50.values[i]:.1f}" for i in show]
print(f"largest cluster: {len(big)} molecules; showing {len(show)}; "
      f"pIC50 spread {data.pIC50.values[list(big)].min():.1f}-{data.pIC50.values[list(big)].max():.1f}")
Draw.MolsToGridImage(gal, molsPerRow=3, subImgSize=(220, 160), legends=legs)

largest cluster: 71 molecules; showing 9; pIC50 spread 5.5-11.5

Figure 13. Nine members of the largest cluster, each labelled with its potency. They are visibly variations on one theme - the same core wearing different substituents - which is what a chemical series looks like. Notice that the potencies are not identical across the series (the printed spread covers more than a log unit): even within one tight cluster, decoration matters, and the most and least potent members differ enough to include a possible activity cliff. The cluster tells you the chemotype; it does not promise uniform activity.

9. Diversity selection: the MaxMin plate

The opposite of finding dense series is deliberately spreading out. When you can only afford to test a handful of compounds - say the 96 wells of a plate - you want them as diverse as possible, so that a single screen samples the whole collection rather than one crowded corner. The standard greedy algorithm is MaxMin[16]: start from one molecule, then repeatedly add the molecule whose minimum distance to everything already picked is largest (the point furthest from the current selection). RDKit implements it directly on fingerprints. In practice a diversity pick is usually combined with a property constraint - selecting, say, only molecules that are reasonably drug-like by a score such as QED[25] - so that the plate is both diverse and worth testing; we keep the two concerns separate here for clarity, and Unit 9 treats drug-likeness filters in full.

# Pick a maximally diverse 'plate' with MaxMin; compare its spread to a random pick of equal size.
PLATE = min(96, N // 2)
picker = MaxMinPicker()
div_idx = list(picker.LazyBitVectorPick(fps, N, PLATE, seed=0))
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rnd_idx = list(rng.choice(N, PLATE, replace=False))
def nn_within(idx):          # nearest-neighbour distance of each picked molecule to the rest of the pick
    sub = D[np.ix_(idx, idx)].copy(); np.fill_diagonal(sub, np.inf)
    return sub.min(axis=1)
nn_div, nn_rnd = nn_within(div_idx), nn_within(rnd_idx)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 3.2))
ax.hist(nn_rnd, bins=20, alpha=0.6, color="#999999", label=f"random pick (mean NN {nn_rnd.mean():.2f})")
ax.hist(nn_div, bins=20, alpha=0.6, color="#d2691e", label=f"MaxMin pick (mean NN {nn_div.mean():.2f})")
ax.set_xlabel("nearest-neighbour Tanimoto distance within the pick"); ax.set_ylabel("molecules")
ax.set_title(f"A diverse {PLATE}-compound plate spreads out more than a random one"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
print(f"mean nearest-neighbour distance - MaxMin {nn_div.mean():.3f} vs random {nn_rnd.mean():.3f}")
fig.tight_layout()

mean nearest-neighbour distance - MaxMin 0.741 vs random 0.447

Figure 14. For each molecule in a pick, its distance to the nearest other molecule in the same pick - large values mean the selection is well spread. The MaxMin plate (orange) is shifted to larger nearest-neighbour distances than a random plate (grey) of the same size, as the printed means confirm: MaxMin deliberately avoids choosing near-duplicates. A random selection, by contrast, tends to over-sample the populous series (it picks proportionally to cluster size) and so wastes wells on compounds that are nearly the same. When every assay well costs money, that difference is the value of a diversity algorithm.

# Where the two picks land on the t-SNE map: MaxMin covers the space, random clumps in dense regions.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 4.4))
for ax, idx, title, col in zip(axes, [div_idx, rnd_idx], ["MaxMin diversity pick", "random pick"], ["#d2691e", "#333333"]):
    ax.scatter(Y[:, 0], Y[:, 1], s=6, color="#dddddd")
    ax.scatter(Y[idx, 0], Y[idx, 1], s=22, color=col, edgecolor="k", linewidth=0.3)
    ax.set_title(f"{title} ({PLATE})"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.suptitle("Diversity pick covers the map; random pick follows the crowd", y=1.02, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 15. The two selections on the t-SNE layout (grey = all molecules). The MaxMin pick (left) scatters across the whole map, reaching into the sparse corners and isolated islands; the random pick (right) concentrates wherever the molecules are dense, leaving outlying regions unsampled. This is the picture to carry away: diversity selection samples chemical space; random selection samples the collection's bias. Which you want depends on the question - diverse for a first exploration, representative (one per Butina cluster) for a balanced follow-up - but the choice should be deliberate.

Where this sits in the course

Chemical-space analysis is rarely the end goal; it is the lens you look through before and after every other step. The clusters you found here define the scaffolds and series dissected in Unit 11, and they are the natural unit for the honest train/test splitting of Unit 14 - putting whole clusters in either training or test (a "scaffold split") is how you stop a model from being graded on near-duplicates of what it has already seen. Colouring a map by activity previews the property prediction of Unit 13, and colouring it by a drug-likeness score such as QED connects to the filters of Unit 9. The diversity pick is how a capstone project (Unit 19) would choose what to make or test next. In short: before you model a collection, map it; after you model it, map the errors.

10. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • What chemical space is, why it is astronomically large, and why we only ever work with a tiny, biased sample of it.
  • Why a fingerprint plus a Tanimoto distance turns a compound collection into a geometry, and why that geometry is sparse and high-dimensional.
  • That PCA gives an interpretable but uninformative map of fingerprints (little variance in any two directions), while t-SNE (and UMAP) give a clearer map by preserving neighbourhoods at the cost of all global meaning.
  • The three rules for reading a t-SNE/UMAP map honestly: cluster size, inter-cluster distance, and apparent cluster count are all untrustworthy.
  • The Taylor-Butina sphere-exclusion algorithm in full - traced by hand and run in code - and how it differs from k-means.
  • How to read a Bemis-Murcko scaffold out of a cluster and recognise a chemical series (the quinazoline EGFR chemotype here).
  • How MaxMin diversity selection spreads a pick across chemical space, and why that beats random selection when assay wells are scarce.

11. Self-assessment

1. Why does a PCA map of Morgan fingerprints usually look like a featureless cloud, with low percentages on both axes?Because fingerprint variance is spread across many directions with no small dominant set, so no two orthogonal linear axes capture much of it. The scree plot shows each successive PC explaining only a small, quickly-shrinking share, and the first two together well under a quarter; PCA therefore reports (correctly) that the data is intrinsically high-dimensional, which is why it cannot give a clean 2-D separation.
2. A colleague says "these two t-SNE clusters are far apart, so the molecules are very different; and the big cluster is more important than the small one." What is wrong?Both claims misread t-SNE. Inter-cluster distances are not meaningful - t-SNE only preserves local neighbourhoods, so far-apart clusters are not necessarily more dissimilar. Cluster sizes are also distorted (dense regions are expanded, sparse ones shrunk), so area on the map does not equal number or importance of molecules.
3. In the hand trace, catechol and aniline are 0.69 apart (more than the 0.65 threshold), yet both end up in the same cluster. How?Sphere exclusion clusters by distance to the centroid, not pairwise. Phenol was the centroid; catechol (0.50) and aniline (0.62) are both within 0.65 of phenol, so both are swept into phenol's sphere even though they are not within 0.65 of each other.
4. Why does Taylor-Butina not require you to choose the number of clusters, whereas k-means does?Butina is threshold-based: you specify a distance cutoff that defines "neighbour", and the number of clusters falls out of the data's density. k-means optimises within-cluster variance for a fixed k that you must set in advance, so it will return exactly k groups whether or not that matches the real structure.
5. What is a Bemis-Murcko scaffold, and what does it mean when a Butina cluster's members share one?It is the molecule reduced to its ring systems plus the linkers between them, with terminal substituents removed. When a cluster's members share a scaffold they form a chemical series - the same core decorated differently - which is the natural unit of a medicinal-chemistry optimisation campaign.
6. The similar-property figure shows activity differences shrinking as similarity rises, but never reaching zero. What are the non-zero cases at high similarity called, and why do they matter?They are activity cliffs: pairs of very similar molecules with very different potencies. They matter because they are precisely where similarity-based prediction and smooth chemical-space maps fail, and because they often pinpoint a key interaction in the binding site (Unit 11).
7. Why is Euclidean distance on raw fingerprint bits a poor choice, and what do we use instead?Fingerprints are sparse (a few dozen of 2048 bits on), so almost any two drug-like molecules share almost no bits and are nearly equidistant in Euclidean terms - the curse of dimensionality. Tanimoto distance (1 minus the intersection-over-union of on-bits) focuses on shared structure and is the standard.
8. You run t-SNE twice with different perplexities and get different-looking maps. Which features should you trust?Trust which molecules group together locally; distrust the number of clusters, their sizes and their relative positions, all of which shift with perplexity. Confirm any grouping with a defined-criterion method (Butina) before drawing conclusions.
9. Why does a random 96-compound pick tend to over-represent the big clusters, and why is that bad for a first screen?Random selection picks each molecule with equal probability, so it draws from a cluster in proportion to that cluster's size - populous series dominate. For a first exploration that wastes wells on near-duplicates and leaves sparse regions untested, so you learn little about the breadth of the collection.
10. The MaxMin algorithm is greedy. In one sentence, what does each step do?Each step adds the molecule whose minimum distance to the already-selected set is the largest - i.e. the point currently furthest from everything picked so far.
11. Our pipeline fed the precomputed Tanimoto distance matrix to t-SNE rather than letting it use Euclidean distance on the bits. Why is that the right choice here?Because Tanimoto is the chemically meaningful similarity for binary fingerprints and is the same distance Butina clusters on; using it keeps the map, the clusters and the diversity pick on one consistent geometry, and avoids the weak Euclidean-on-sparse-bits distance.
12. UMAP did not run in this build. Did we lose anything pedagogically, and what is the general lesson?No - the three reading rules (size, inter-cluster distance and apparent count are untrustworthy) apply to UMAP just as to t-SNE, and the t-SNE map already demonstrates them. The general lesson is that every non-linear projection trades global faithfulness for local clarity, so all of them are hypothesis generators to be confirmed by a defined-criterion method.

Glossary

Activity cliff
A pair of structurally very similar molecules with very different activity; the main failure of the similar-property principle.
Bemis-Murcko scaffold
A molecule reduced to its ring systems plus connecting linkers, with terminal substituents removed; the shared core of a series.
Chemical space
The set of all possible molecules with a notion of similarity; the chemist's feature space.
Cluster centroid
In Taylor-Butina, the most-connected molecule of a cluster, used as its representative (a real molecule, unlike a k-means mean).
Dimensionality reduction
Mapping high-dimensional vectors to a few dimensions while preserving some structure (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP).
Diversity selection
Choosing a subset that spreads across chemical space (e.g. MaxMin), as opposed to a representative or random subset.
IC50 / pIC50
The concentration halving a target's activity; pIC50 = -log10(IC50 in molar) puts potency on a convenient log scale.
MaxMin
A greedy diversity algorithm: repeatedly add the molecule furthest (in minimum distance) from those already chosen.
Morgan fingerprint
A fixed-length bit vector recording circular atom environments; the vector representation used throughout.
PCA
Principal Component Analysis; a linear projection onto the directions of greatest variance.
Perplexity
The t-SNE hyperparameter setting the effective neighbourhood size; it changes the resulting map.
Scaffold / series / chemotype
A shared molecular core; a family of molecules built on one core; the type of core - all names for the structure a cluster captures.
Sphere exclusion
The idea behind Taylor-Butina: claim the densest sphere, exclude its members, repeat.
Tanimoto distance
1 minus the Tanimoto similarity (intersection over union of on-bits); the distance used for maps and clusters.
t-SNE / UMAP
Non-linear neighbour-preserving embeddings that reveal local clusters but distort global geometry.
